expectedText:
EMPLOYER-CONTROLLED TIME: EXIT SEARCHES, MANDATORY TRANSPORTATION, AND OFF-THE-CLOCK MINUTES — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Acme, Inc. maintains this information sheet to describe how California law treats certain periods of time that fall outside an hourly employee's scheduled shift but that the employer nonetheless directs or controls — for example, time Jordan Lee or any other nonexempt employee spends waiting for and undergoing a required exit search of bags or personal devices, time spent riding employer-mandated transportation to a worksite, time spent awaiting a vehicle inspection at a security gate, and small amounts of work performed after clocking out. The California Supreme Court has addressed each of these situations under the "hours worked" definition in the Industrial Welfare Commission's wage orders. This document states what the Court decided in those cases and what it expressly left undecided. It is limited to the control-based compensability of these activities; it does not address on-call or standby time before an employee is called in (covered by the separate On-Call and Standby Time Compensability information sheet), reporting-time pay for shifts that are cut short (covered by the separate Reporting Time Pay information sheet), or the rounding of time punches (covered by the separate Time Clock Rounding Practices information sheet).

THE WAGE ORDER DEFINITION OF "HOURS WORKED" AND ITS TWO CLAUSES
Each Industrial Welfare Commission wage order requires that employees be paid for all "hours worked," and defines that term. In Wage Order No. 7-2001 (the mercantile industry order at issue in Frlekin v. Apple Inc.), section 2(G) defines "hours worked" as the time during which an employee is subject to the control of an employer, and includes all the time the employee is suffered or permitted to work, whether or not required to do so. The California Supreme Court has described this definition as containing two separate clauses: a "control" clause (time during which the employee is subject to the employer's control) and a "suffered or permitted to work" clause. The same two-clause definition appears in the other wage orders, differing only in subdivision lettering — for example, section 2(J) of Wage Order No. 16 (construction, drilling, logging, and mining on-site occupations) and section 2(G) of the former Wage Order No. 14-80 (agricultural occupations) were the provisions at issue in Huerta and Morillion, respectively.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "means the time during which an employee is subject to the control of an employer, and includes all the time the employee is suffered or permitted to work, whether or not required to do so."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 7-2001, § 2(G), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11070, subd. 2(G) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle7.pdf)
  "“Hours worked” is defined as “the time during which an employee is subject to the control of an employer, and includes all the time the employee is suffered or permitted to work, whether or not required to do so.” (Id., § 11070, subd. 2(G).)"
  — Frlekin v. Apple Inc., 8 Cal. 5th 1038 (Cal. 2020) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4726983/frlekin-v-apple-inc/)
  Known gap: The quoted definition is taken from the Department of Industrial Relations' posted text of Wage Order No. 7-2001, in which the term "Hours worked" is set off by non-standard quotation glyphs that the PDF text extraction rendered as the characters ― and ‖; the quote begins after those glyphs (at the word "means") to avoid reproducing the extraction artifact. This clause does not address the health care industry variant of the definition found in Wage Orders 4 and 5, which is described in the separate On-Call and Standby Time Compensability information sheet. Whether a particular industry or occupation is governed by Wage Order 7 or another order is outside this document's scope.

THE CONTROL CLAUSE CAN BE SATISFIED ON ITS OWN
In Morillion v. Royal Packing Co., the California Supreme Court held that the two clauses of the "hours worked" definition operate independently, so that time may be compensable under the control clause alone even if the employee is not performing work during that time. The Court reasoned that the word "includes," which introduces the "suffered or permitted to work" language, is a term of enlargement: the definition of "hours worked" is expanded by, rather than limited to, the time an employee is suffered or permitted to work. On that basis the Court concluded that the employees' compulsory travel time could be compensable under the control language alone, rejecting the Court of Appeal's view that such a reading would ignore the "suffered or permitted to work" clause.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "the definition of "hours worked" is expanded by, rather than limited to, the time spent when an employee is "suffered or permitted to work.""
  — Morillion v. Royal Packing Co., 22 Cal. 4th 575 (Cal. 2000) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1291367/morillion-v-royal-packing-co/)
  "In determining that plaintiffs' compulsory travel time may be compensable under just the "control" language, we do not agree with the Court of Appeal that we would be ignoring the "suffered or permitted to work" language of the "hours worked" definition."
  — Morillion v. Royal Packing Co., 22 Cal. 4th 575 (Cal. 2000) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1291367/morillion-v-royal-packing-co/)
  Known gap: Morillion interpreted the "hours worked" definition in the agricultural wage order in effect at the time (Wage Order No. 14-80); the Court and later decisions have treated the definition as materially identical across the wage orders, but this clause does not independently verify the text of every wage order. The Morillion opinion text was obtained from CourtListener's HTML rendering (its plain-text field was empty), so the quotations use straight rather than typographic quotation marks as they appear in that rendering.

EMPLOYER-MANDATED TRANSPORTATION: THE MORILLION HOLDING
Morillion involved agricultural employees who were required to meet at designated departure points and ride their employer's buses to and from the fields, and who were prohibited from driving themselves. The California Supreme Court held that when an employer requires its employees to meet at designated places to take its buses to work and prohibits them from taking their own transportation, the employees are subject to the control of the employer, and their time spent traveling on the buses is compensable as "hours worked." The Court found that this compulsory travel time included the time the employees spent waiting for the buses to begin transporting them. In reaching that result the Court stated the principle that later decisions have repeatedly reaffirmed: the level of the employer's control over its employees, rather than the mere fact that the employer requires the employees' activity, is determinative.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "When an employer requires its employees to meet at designated places to take its buses to work and prohibits them from taking their own transportation, these employees are "subject to the control of an employer," and their time spent traveling on the buses is compensable as "hours worked.""
  — Morillion v. Royal Packing Co., 22 Cal. 4th 575 (Cal. 2000) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1291367/morillion-v-royal-packing-co/)
  "we find that plaintiffs' compulsory travel time, which includes the time they spent waiting for Royal's buses to begin transporting them, was compensable."
  — Morillion v. Royal Packing Co., 22 Cal. 4th 575 (Cal. 2000) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1291367/morillion-v-royal-packing-co/)
  "The level of the employer's control over its employees, rather than the mere fact that the employer requires the employees' activity, is determinative."
  — Morillion v. Royal Packing Co., 22 Cal. 4th 575, 587 (Cal. 2000) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1291367/morillion-v-royal-packing-co/)
  Known gap: The pin citation to page 587 for the "level of the employer's control" sentence is taken from the California Supreme Court's own citation of that passage in Frlekin v. Apple Inc. ("Id. at p. 587"), not from reporter pagination in the CourtListener text, which carries star pagination for the Cal.Rptr.2d parallel reporter rather than the official Cal.4th reporter. The remaining Morillion quotations are cited to the opinion's starting page only.

COMPULSORY TRAVEL TIME DISTINGUISHED FROM THE ORDINARY COMMUTE
Morillion drew a line between travel that the employer controls and requires and an ordinary commute that employees take on their own. The Court adopted the term "compulsory travel time" specifically to distinguish between travel to and from a work site that an employer controls and requires, and an ordinary commute from home to work and back that employees take on their own. Applying that distinction, the Court stated that compulsory travel time did not include the time the employees spent commuting from home to the bus departure points and from the departure points back home again. The Court also explained that employees who commute on their own may choose the time and route of their travel and may run errands or leave early for personal appointments, which is the kind of freedom the employer's compulsory transportation removed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "we adopt this reference to distinguish between travel to and from a work site that an employer controls and requires, and an ordinary commute from home to work and back that employees take on their own. Accordingly, this compulsory travel time does not include the time plaintiffs spent commuting from home to the departure points and from the departure points back again."
  — Morillion v. Royal Packing Co., 22 Cal. 4th 575 (Cal. 2000) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1291367/morillion-v-royal-packing-co/)
  "By commuting on their own, employees may choose and may be able to run errands before work and to leave from work early for personal appointments."
  — Morillion v. Royal Packing Co., 22 Cal. 4th 575 (Cal. 2000) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1291367/morillion-v-royal-packing-co/)
  Known gap: This clause states Morillion's distinction as the Court drew it on the facts before it (employer-required buses with self-transportation prohibited). Morillion contrasted a federal case in which employees were free to choose whether to ride employer buses and treated that voluntariness as dispositive; that contrast is described in prose here rather than quoted because the CourtListener HTML rendering of that sentence dropped the dashes around the phrase "rather than required," producing a run-together word that could not be reproduced verbatim. How the distinction applies to employer-provided transportation that employees are permitted but not required to use is not resolved by this document.

REQUIRED EXIT SEARCHES OF BAGS AND PERSONAL DEVICES: THE FRLEKIN HOLDING
In Frlekin v. Apple Inc., the California Supreme Court answered a question certified by the Ninth Circuit about Apple's retail-store policy requiring employees to have their bags, packages, and personal Apple devices searched by a manager or security before leaving the store. The certified question, as reformulated by the Court, was whether time spent on the employer's premises waiting for, and undergoing, required exit searches of packages, bags, or personal technology devices voluntarily brought to work purely for personal convenience by employees is compensable as "hours worked" within the meaning of Wage Order 7. The Court answered yes. Its disposition states that the employees' time spent on Apple's premises waiting for, and undergoing, mandatory exit searches of bags, packages, or personal Apple technology devices, such as iPhones, voluntarily brought to work purely for personal convenience is compensable as "hours worked" within the meaning of Wage Order 7.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Is time spent on the employer’s premises waiting for, and undergoing, required exit searches of packages, bags, or personal technology devices voluntarily brought to work purely for personal convenience by employees compensable as “hours worked” within the meaning of Wage Order 7? For the reasons that follow, we conclude the answer to the certified question is, yes."
  — Frlekin v. Apple Inc., 8 Cal. 5th 1038 (Cal. 2020) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4726983/frlekin-v-apple-inc/)
  "We conclude that plaintiffs’ time spent on Apple’s premises waiting for, and undergoing, mandatory exit searches of bags, packages, or personal Apple technology devices, such as iPhones, voluntarily brought to work purely for personal convenience is compensable as “hours worked” within the meaning of Wage Order 7."
  — Frlekin v. Apple Inc., 8 Cal. 5th 1038 (Cal. 2020) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4726983/frlekin-v-apple-inc/)
  Known gap: Frlekin decided the compensability question under Wage Order 7 (mercantile industry) on the facts certified by the Ninth Circuit, in which the searches were performed on the employer's premises and employees could not leave without submitting to them. The Court's opinion notes that the employer remains free to narrow or broaden its search policy and to reduce search time through staffing or technology, which is described in the factors clause below. This clause does not address search policies in other industries or searches conducted off the employer's premises.

THE FACTORS COURTS CONSIDER FOR ONSITE, EMPLOYER-CONTROLLED ACTIVITIES
Frlekin reaffirmed Morillion's rule that the level of the employer's control over its employees, rather than the mere fact that the employer requires the employees' activity, is determinative of whether an activity is compensable under the control clause. The Court added that whether an activity is required remains probative, but that — at least for onsite, employer-controlled activities — the mandatory nature of the activity is not the only factor. Courts may and should consider additional relevant factors, including but not limited to the location of the activity, the degree of the employer's control, whether the activity primarily benefits the employee or the employer, and whether the activity is enforced through disciplinary measures. Applying those factors, the Court found that Apple's exit searches were required as a practical matter, occurred at the workplace, involved a significant degree of control, were imposed primarily for Apple's benefit, and were enforced through the threat of discipline. The Court also observed that Apple could tailor its bag-search policy as narrowly or broadly as it wished and could minimize search time by hiring sufficient security personnel or employing adequate security technology, but that it had to compensate employees to whom the policy applied for the time spent waiting for and undergoing the searches.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "In sum, we reaffirm our holding in Morillion that “[t]he level of the employer’s control over its employees, rather than the mere fact that the employer requires the employees’ activity, is determinative” concerning whether an activity is compensable under the “hours worked” control clause."
  — Frlekin v. Apple Inc., 8 Cal. 5th 1038 (Cal. 2020) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4726983/frlekin-v-apple-inc/)
  "We conclude that courts may and should consider additional relevant factors — including, but not limited to, the location of the activity, the degree of the employer’s control, whether the activity primarily benefits the employee or employer, and whether the activity is enforced through disciplinary measures"
  — Frlekin v. Apple Inc., 8 Cal. 5th 1038 (Cal. 2020) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4726983/frlekin-v-apple-inc/)
  "Apple’s exit searches are required as a practical matter, occur at the workplace, involve a significant degree of control, are imposed primarily for Apple’s benefit, and are enforced through threat of discipline."
  — Frlekin v. Apple Inc., 8 Cal. 5th 1038 (Cal. 2020) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4726983/frlekin-v-apple-inc/)
  "We reiterate that Apple may tailor its bag-search policy as narrowly or broadly as it desires and may minimize the time required for exit searches by hiring sufficient security personnel or employing adequate security technology."
  — Frlekin v. Apple Inc., 8 Cal. 5th 1038 (Cal. 2020) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4726983/frlekin-v-apple-inc/)
  Known gap: The factors quotation is cut off after the words "disciplinary measures" because the remainder of the Court's sentence ("when evaluating such employer-controlled conduct") is broken across a line in the slip-opinion text with a hyphenation artifact ("employer- controlled") that cannot be reproduced verbatim; the omitted words are paraphrased in the body. Frlekin's factor list is expressly non-exhaustive ("including, but not limited to"), and the Court framed it as applying to onsite employer-controlled activities; whether and how these factors apply to offsite activities was not decided.

FRLEKIN APPLIES RETROACTIVELY; THE "SUFFERED OR PERMITTED" QUESTION WAS LEFT OPEN
Apple asked the Court to apply its holding prospectively only, arguing that it had reasonably relied on Morillion as establishing that purely voluntary activities are not employer control. The Court rejected that argument, explaining that Morillion addressed compulsory employer-provided transportation and did not hold that an employer-controlled activity must be unavoidably required in order to count as "hours worked," so Apple could not claim reasonable reliance on settled law. The Court saw no reason to depart from the general rule that judicial decisions apply retroactively. Separately, because the Court found the search time compensable under the control clause, it expressed no view on the employees' alternative argument that the same time was compensable under the "suffered or permitted to work" clause.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Morillion addressed compulsory employer-provided transportation to and from work. (Morillion, supra, 22 Cal.4th at p. 578.) It did not, as Apple contends, hold that any employer-controlled activity must be unavoidably required in order to be compensable as “hours worked.”"
  — Frlekin v. Apple Inc., 8 Cal. 5th 1038 (Cal. 2020) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4726983/frlekin-v-apple-inc/)
  "Accordingly, we see no reason to depart from the general rule that judicial decisions apply retroactively."
  — Frlekin v. Apple Inc., 8 Cal. 5th 1038 (Cal. 2020) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4726983/frlekin-v-apple-inc/)
  "Because we have concluded that plaintiffs are entitled to compensation under the control clause, we express no view concerning plaintiffs’ alternative argument that the searches are compensable under the “suffered or permitted to work” clause."
  — Frlekin v. Apple Inc., 8 Cal. 5th 1038 (Cal. 2020) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4726983/frlekin-v-apple-inc/)
  Known gap: The retroactivity ruling means Frlekin's holding governs conduct that predates the February 13, 2020 decision, subject to any applicable limitations periods, which this document does not address. The Court's statement that it expressed no view on the "suffered or permitted to work" clause is a limitation on the reach of Frlekin's reasoning, not a holding that exit-search time is or is not compensable under that clause.

VEHICLE SECURITY GATES AND EXIT INSPECTIONS: THE HUERTA HOLDING
In Huerta v. CSI Electrical Contractors, decided in 2024, the California Supreme Court applied the control clause to a construction worksite with a single security gate. Workers drove their personal vehicles to the gate, where guards scanned badges and sometimes looked inside vehicles and truck beds; at the end of the day workers again lined up at the gate for an exit procedure that could take a minute or more per vehicle and caused delays of five to over 30 minutes. The Court held that an employee's time spent on an employer's premises awaiting and undergoing an employer-mandated exit procedure that includes the employer's visual inspection of the employee's personal vehicle is compensable as "hours worked" within the meaning of Wage Order No. 16, section 2(J).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "The exit procedure could take up to a minute or more per vehicle and caused delays of five to over 30 minutes."
  — Huerta v. CSI Electrical Contractors, Cal. Supreme Court No. S275431 (Cal. Mar. 25, 2024) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9487447/huerta-v-csi-electrical-contractors/)
  "First, an employee’s time spent on an employer’s premises awaiting and undergoing an employer-mandated exit procedure that includes the employer’s visual inspection of the employee’s personal vehicle is compensable as “hours worked” within the meaning of Wage Order No. 16, section 2(J)."
  — Huerta v. CSI Electrical Contractors, Cal. Supreme Court No. S275431 (Cal. Mar. 25, 2024) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9487447/huerta-v-csi-electrical-contractors/)
  Known gap: Huerta answered questions certified by the Ninth Circuit under Wage Order No. 16 (on-site occupations in construction, drilling, logging, and mining); the "hours worked" definition it applied is the same two-clause definition found in the other wage orders. This clause cites the opinion by California Supreme Court docket number and decision date because the CourtListener record fetched for this document did not carry an official reporter citation, and no reporter citation was independently verified. The description of the gate procedure is taken from the Court's recitation of the facts as certified by the Ninth Circuit.

DRIVING BETWEEN A SECURITY GATE AND PARKING LOT UNDER ORDINARY WORKPLACE RULES
Huerta also addressed the time employees spent driving their personal vehicles between the security gate and the employee parking lots while subject to site rules such as a 20-mile-per-hour speed limit and a prohibition on playing music that could be heard outside the vehicle. The Court gave two distinct answers. First, that travel is not compensable as "hours worked" under the control clause, because an employer's imposition of ordinary workplace rules on employees during their drive to the worksite in a personal vehicle does not create the requisite level of employer control. Second, the same travel may nonetheless be compensable under a separate provision found in Wage Order No. 16, section 5(A), which requires payment for all employer-mandated travel that occurs after the first location where the employee's presence is required by the employer. The Court held that the drive between the security gate and the parking lots is compensable as employer-mandated travel under section 5(A) if the security gate was the first location where the employee's presence was required for an employment-related reason other than the practical necessity of accessing the worksite.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Separately, this travel time is not compensable as “hours worked” because an employer’s imposition of ordinary workplace rules on employees during their drive to the worksite in a personal vehicle does not create the requisite level of employer control."
  — Huerta v. CSI Electrical Contractors, Cal. Supreme Court No. S275431 (Cal. Mar. 25, 2024) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9487447/huerta-v-csi-electrical-contractors/)
  "Second, the time that an employee spends traveling between the Security Gate and the employee parking lots is compensable as “employer-mandated travel” under Wage Order No. 16, section 5(A)"
  — Huerta v. CSI Electrical Contractors, Cal. Supreme Court No. S275431 (Cal. Mar. 25, 2024) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9487447/huerta-v-csi-electrical-contractors/)
  Known gap: The section 5(A) employer-mandated-travel provision discussed in Huerta is specific to Wage Order No. 16; the Court's second answer therefore does not translate directly to employees governed by other wage orders that lack an equivalent provision. The section 5(A) holding is quoted from the opinion's introductory answer only through the words "section 5(A)" because the remainder of that sentence contains a slip-opinion line-break hyphenation artifact ("employment- related") that cannot be reproduced verbatim; the condition the Court attached (first location required for an employment-related reason other than the practical necessity of accessing the worksite) is paraphrased in the body. The characterization of the specific rules in effect during the drive (the speed limit and music restriction) is drawn from the opinion's statement of facts and is summarized rather than quoted.

UNPAID MEAL PERIODS SPENT CONFINED TO THE PREMISES
The third question in Huerta concerned employees covered by a collective bargaining agreement that satisfied Labor Code section 512, subdivision (e), and Wage Order No. 16, section 10(E), and that provided for an unpaid meal period, where the employer prohibited employees from leaving the premises during that period. The Court held that such time is nonetheless compensable under the wage order as "hours worked" if the employer prohibits the employee from leaving the employer's premises or a designated area during the meal period and if this prohibition prevents the employee from engaging in otherwise feasible personal activities. The Court added that an employee may bring an action under Labor Code section 1194 to enforce the wage order and recover unpaid wages for that time.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "that time is nonetheless compensable under the wage order as “hours worked” if the employer prohibits the employee from leaving the employer’s premises or a designated area during the meal period and if this prohibition prevents the employee from engaging in otherwise feasible personal activities. An employee may bring an action under Labor Code section 1194 to enforce the wage order and recover unpaid wages for that time."
  — Huerta v. CSI Electrical Contractors, Cal. Supreme Court No. S275431 (Cal. Mar. 25, 2024) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9487447/huerta-v-csi-electrical-contractors/)
  Known gap: This holding is framed around the collective-bargaining exemption in Labor Code section 512(e) and Wage Order 16 section 10(E); the Court's point was that a qualifying agreement's designation of a meal period as unpaid does not override the wage order's requirement to pay for time during which the employee remains under the employer's control. The general rules for meal periods outside that setting, including the premium pay for missed meal periods, are covered by the corpus's separate meal and rest break documents and are not restated here.

SMALL AMOUNTS OF OFF-THE-CLOCK WORK: THE TROESTER HOLDING
Federal courts applying the Fair Labor Standards Act have sometimes excused payment for small amounts of otherwise compensable time under a "de minimis" doctrine, on a showing that the bits of time are administratively difficult to record. In Troester v. Starbucks Corp., the California Supreme Court answered a certified question about whether that federal doctrine applies to claims for unpaid wages under California Labor Code sections 510, 1194, and 1197. The facts involved a shift supervisor whom the employer's software required to clock out before running the store-closing procedure, activating the alarm, locking the door, and walking coworkers to their cars, amounting to several minutes of unpaid work per closing shift. The Court held that the relevant California statutes and wage order have not incorporated the FLSA de minimis doctrine, and that although California has a de minimis rule as a background principle of state law, that rule did not apply on these facts. The Court stated that the relevant statutes and wage order do not allow employers to require employees to routinely work for minutes off the clock without compensation, and observed that a few extra minutes of work each day can add up.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Federal courts have applied the doctrine in some circumstances to excuse the payment of wages for small amounts of otherwise compensable time upon a showing that the bits of time are administratively difficult to record."
  — Troester v. Starbucks Corp., 5 Cal. 5th 829 (Cal. 2018) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4520879/troester-v-starbucks-corporation/)
  "We hold that the relevant California statutes and wage order have not incorporated the de minimis doctrine found in the FLSA. We further conclude that although California has a de minimis rule that is a background principle of state law, the rule is not applicable to the regularly reoccurring activities that are principally at issue here."
  — Troester v. Starbucks Corp., 5 Cal. 5th 829 (Cal. 2018) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4520879/troester-v-starbucks-corporation/)
  "As the facts here demonstrate, a few extra minutes of work each day can add up."
  — Troester v. Starbucks Corp., 5 Cal. 5th 829 (Cal. 2018) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4520879/troester-v-starbucks-corporation/)
  Known gap: The Court's concluding sentence about routine off-the-clock minutes is not quoted verbatim because the slip-opinion text breaks the word "off-the-clock" across a line ("off-the- clock"); it is paraphrased in the body. Troester's holding is limited to regularly occurring off-the-clock work of the kind before the Court; the next clause states what the Court expressly left open regarding irregular or very brief activities.

WHAT TROESTER LEFT OPEN, AND THE ALTERNATIVES THE COURT IDENTIFIED
Troester expressly left open whether there are wage claims involving employee activities that are so irregular or brief in duration that it would not be reasonable to require employers to compensate employees for the time spent on them. In declining to adopt the federal doctrine for regularly occurring work, the Court pointed to alternatives to leaving the time unpaid: restructuring the work so that employees do not have to work before or after clocking out; using technological advances that may help with tracking small amounts of time, including customizing available time-tracking tools or developing new ones; and, where neither restructuring nor a technological fix is practical, reasonably estimating work time — for example, through surveys, time studies, or a fair rounding policy — and compensating employees for that time. The Court declined to adopt a rule that would require the employee to bear the entire burden of any difficulty in recording regularly occurring work time.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "We leave open whether there are wage claims involving employee activities that are so irregular or brief in duration that employers may not be reasonably required to compensate employees for the time spent on them."
  — Troester v. Starbucks Corp., 5 Cal. 5th 829 (Cal. 2018) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4520879/troester-v-starbucks-corporation/)
  "technological advances may help with tracking small amounts of time. An employer may be able to customize and adapt available time tracking tools or develop new ones when no off-the-shelf product meets its needs. And even when neither a restructuring of work nor a technological fix is practical, it may be possible to reasonably estimate work time — for example, through surveys, time studies, or, as See’s Candy suggested, a fair rounding policy — and to compensate employees for that time."
  — Troester v. Starbucks Corp., 5 Cal. 5th 829 (Cal. 2018) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4520879/troester-v-starbucks-corporation/)
  Known gap: The alternatives described here are the Court's own observations about how the recording difficulty that motivated the federal doctrine can be addressed; they are not a list of legal requirements, and the Court did not hold that any particular method must be used. The reference to a "fair rounding policy" points to See's Candy Shops, Inc. v. Superior Court, whose rounding standard — and the later limits placed on it — are described in the separate Time Clock Rounding Practices information sheet.

HOW UNPAID TIME UNDER THE CONTROL CLAUSE IS RECOVERED: LABOR CODE SECTION 1194
Time that qualifies as "hours worked" under the control clause must be paid at no less than the applicable minimum wage and, where it pushes the employee past the daily or weekly overtime thresholds, at the applicable overtime rate. Labor Code section 1194, subdivision (a), provides that, notwithstanding any agreement to work for a lesser wage, any employee receiving less than the legal minimum wage or the legal overtime compensation applicable to the employee is entitled to recover in a civil action the unpaid balance of the full amount of that minimum wage or overtime compensation, including interest, reasonable attorney's fees, and costs of suit. The California Supreme Court in Huerta identified section 1194 as the vehicle by which an employee may enforce the wage order and recover unpaid wages for time spent under the employer's control, and Troester was itself framed as a question about claims under sections 510, 1194, and 1197.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Notwithstanding any agreement to work for a lesser wage, any employee receiving less than the legal minimum wage or the legal overtime compensation applicable to the employee is entitled to recover in a civil action the unpaid balance of the full amount of this minimum wage or overtime compensation, including interest thereon, reasonable attorney’s fees, and costs of suit."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1194(a), Cal. Lab. Code § 1194, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1194.)
  "An employee may bring an action under Labor Code section 1194 to enforce the wage order and recover unpaid wages for that time."
  — Huerta v. CSI Electrical Contractors, Cal. Supreme Court No. S275431 (Cal. Mar. 25, 2024) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9487447/huerta-v-csi-electrical-contractors/)
  Known gap: Section 1194 is the civil-action remedy; wage claims may also be pursued administratively before the Labor Commissioner, and other Labor Code provisions (for example, liquidated damages under section 1194.2 and civil penalties under the Private Attorneys General Act) may be implicated but are not covered here. The overtime calculation rules themselves are described in the separate California Overtime Pay Calculation information sheet.

expectedJSON.body: Acme, Inc. maintains this information sheet to describe how California law treats certain periods of time that fall outside an hourly employee's scheduled shift but that the employer nonetheless directs or controls — for example, time Jordan Lee or any other nonexempt employee spends waiting for and undergoing a required exit search of bags or personal devices, time spent riding employer-mandated transportation to a worksite, time spent awaiting a vehicle inspection at a security gate, and small amounts of work performed after clocking out. The California Supreme Court has addressed each of these situations under the "hours worked" definition in the Industrial Welfare Commission's wage orders. This document states what the Court decided in those cases and what it expressly left undecided. It is limited to the control-based compensability of these activities; it does not address on-call or standby time before an employee is called in (covered by the separate On-Call and Standby Time Compensability information sheet), reporting-time pay for shifts that are cut short (covered by the separate Reporting Time Pay information sheet), or the rounding of time punches (covered by the separate Time Clock Rounding Practices information sheet).

Each Industrial Welfare Commission wage order requires that employees be paid for all "hours worked," and defines that term. In Wage Order No. 7-2001 (the mercantile industry order at issue in Frlekin v. Apple Inc.), section 2(G) defines "hours worked" as the time during which an employee is subject to the control of an employer, and includes all the time the employee is suffered or permitted to work, whether or not required to do so. The California Supreme Court has described this definition as containing two separate clauses: a "control" clause (time during which the employee is subject to the employer's control) and a "suffered or permitted to work" clause. The same two-clause definition appears in the other wage orders, differing only in subdivision lettering — for example, section 2(J) of Wage Order No. 16 (construction, drilling, logging, and mining on-site occupations) and section 2(G) of the former Wage Order No. 14-80 (agricultural occupations) were the provisions at issue in Huerta and Morillion, respectively.

citations.quote: means the time during which an employee is subject to the control of an employer, and includes all the time the employee is suffered or permitted to work, whether or not required to do so.

“Hours worked” is defined as “the time during which an employee is subject to the control of an employer, and includes all the time the employee is suffered or permitted to work, whether or not required to do so.” (Id., § 11070, subd. 2(G).)

expectedJSON.gap: The quoted definition is taken from the Department of Industrial Relations' posted text of Wage Order No. 7-2001, in which the term "Hours worked" is set off by non-standard quotation glyphs that the PDF text extraction rendered as the characters ― and ‖; the quote begins after those glyphs (at the word "means") to avoid reproducing the extraction artifact. This clause does not address the health care industry variant of the definition found in Wage Orders 4 and 5, which is described in the separate On-Call and Standby Time Compensability information sheet. Whether a particular industry or occupation is governed by Wage Order 7 or another order is outside this document's scope.

expectedJSON.body: In Morillion v. Royal Packing Co., the California Supreme Court held that the two clauses of the "hours worked" definition operate independently, so that time may be compensable under the control clause alone even if the employee is not performing work during that time. The Court reasoned that the word "includes," which introduces the "suffered or permitted to work" language, is a term of enlargement: the definition of "hours worked" is expanded by, rather than limited to, the time an employee is suffered or permitted to work. On that basis the Court concluded that the employees' compulsory travel time could be compensable under the control language alone, rejecting the Court of Appeal's view that such a reading would ignore the "suffered or permitted to work" clause.

citations.quote: the definition of "hours worked" is expanded by, rather than limited to, the time spent when an employee is "suffered or permitted to work."

In determining that plaintiffs' compulsory travel time may be compensable under just the "control" language, we do not agree with the Court of Appeal that we would be ignoring the "suffered or permitted to work" language of the "hours worked" definition.

expectedJSON.gap: Morillion interpreted the "hours worked" definition in the agricultural wage order in effect at the time (Wage Order No. 14-80); the Court and later decisions have treated the definition as materially identical across the wage orders, but this clause does not independently verify the text of every wage order. The Morillion opinion text was obtained from CourtListener's HTML rendering (its plain-text field was empty), so the quotations use straight rather than typographic quotation marks as they appear in that rendering.

expectedJSON.body: Morillion involved agricultural employees who were required to meet at designated departure points and ride their employer's buses to and from the fields, and who were prohibited from driving themselves. The California Supreme Court held that when an employer requires its employees to meet at designated places to take its buses to work and prohibits them from taking their own transportation, the employees are subject to the control of the employer, and their time spent traveling on the buses is compensable as "hours worked." The Court found that this compulsory travel time included the time the employees spent waiting for the buses to begin transporting them. In reaching that result the Court stated the principle that later decisions have repeatedly reaffirmed: the level of the employer's control over its employees, rather than the mere fact that the employer requires the employees' activity, is determinative.

citations.quote: When an employer requires its employees to meet at designated places to take its buses to work and prohibits them from taking their own transportation, these employees are "subject to the control of an employer," and their time spent traveling on the buses is compensable as "hours worked."
we find that plaintiffs' compulsory travel time, which includes the time they spent waiting for Royal's buses to begin transporting them, was compensable.
The level of the employer's control over its employees, rather than the mere fact that the employer requires the employees' activity, is determinative.

expectedJSON.gap: The pin citation to page 587 for the "level of the employer's control" sentence is taken from the California Supreme Court's own citation of that passage in Frlekin v. Apple Inc. ("Id. at p. 587"), not from reporter pagination in the CourtListener text, which carries star pagination for the Cal.Rptr.2d parallel reporter rather than the official Cal.4th reporter. The remaining Morillion quotations are cited to the opinion's starting page only.

expectedJSON.body: Morillion drew a line between travel that the employer controls and requires and an ordinary commute that employees take on their own. The Court adopted the term "compulsory travel time" specifically to distinguish between travel to and from a work site that an employer controls and requires, and an ordinary commute from home to work and back that employees take on their own. Applying that distinction, the Court stated that compulsory travel time did not include the time the employees spent commuting from home to the bus departure points and from the departure points back home again. The Court also explained that employees who commute on their own may choose the time and route of their travel and may run errands or leave early for personal appointments, which is the kind of freedom the employer's compulsory transportation removed.

citations.quote: we adopt this reference to distinguish between travel to and from a work site that an employer controls and requires, and an ordinary commute from home to work and back that employees take on their own. Accordingly, this compulsory travel time does not include the time plaintiffs spent commuting from home to the departure points and from the departure points back again.
By commuting on their own, employees may choose and may be able to run errands before work and to leave from work early for personal appointments.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states Morillion's distinction as the Court drew it on the facts before it (employer-required buses with self-transportation prohibited). Morillion contrasted a federal case in which employees were free to choose whether to ride employer buses and treated that voluntariness as dispositive; that contrast is described in prose here rather than quoted because the CourtListener HTML rendering of that sentence dropped the dashes around the phrase "rather than required," producing a run-together word that could not be reproduced verbatim. How the distinction applies to employer-provided transportation that employees are permitted but not required to use is not resolved by this document.

expectedJSON.body: In Frlekin v. Apple Inc., the California Supreme Court answered a question certified by the Ninth Circuit about Apple's retail-store policy requiring employees to have their bags, packages, and personal Apple devices searched by a manager or security before leaving the store. The certified question, as reformulated by the Court, was whether time spent on the employer's premises waiting for, and undergoing, required exit searches of packages, bags, or personal technology devices voluntarily brought to work purely for personal convenience by employees is compensable as "hours worked" within the meaning of Wage Order 7. The Court answered yes. Its disposition states that the employees' time spent on Apple's premises waiting for, and undergoing, mandatory exit searches of bags, packages, or personal Apple technology devices, such as iPhones, voluntarily brought to work purely for personal convenience is compensable as "hours worked" within the meaning of Wage Order 7.

citations.quote: Is time spent on the employer’s premises waiting for, and undergoing, required exit searches of packages, bags, or personal technology devices voluntarily brought to work purely for personal convenience by employees compensable as “hours worked” within the meaning of Wage Order 7? For the reasons that follow, we conclude the answer to the certified question is, yes.

We conclude that plaintiffs’ time spent on Apple’s premises waiting for, and undergoing, mandatory exit searches of bags, packages, or personal Apple technology devices, such as iPhones, voluntarily brought to work purely for personal convenience is compensable as “hours worked” within the meaning of Wage Order 7.

expectedJSON.gap: Frlekin decided the compensability question under Wage Order 7 (mercantile industry) on the facts certified by the Ninth Circuit, in which the searches were performed on the employer's premises and employees could not leave without submitting to them. The Court's opinion notes that the employer remains free to narrow or broaden its search policy and to reduce search time through staffing or technology, which is described in the factors clause below. This clause does not address search policies in other industries or searches conducted off the employer's premises.

expectedJSON.body: Frlekin reaffirmed Morillion's rule that the level of the employer's control over its employees, rather than the mere fact that the employer requires the employees' activity, is determinative of whether an activity is compensable under the control clause. The Court added that whether an activity is required remains probative, but that — at least for onsite, employer-controlled activities — the mandatory nature of the activity is not the only factor. Courts may and should consider additional relevant factors, including but not limited to the location of the activity, the degree of the employer's control, whether the activity primarily benefits the employee or the employer, and whether the activity is enforced through disciplinary measures. Applying those factors, the Court found that Apple's exit searches were required as a practical matter, occurred at the workplace, involved a significant degree of control, were imposed primarily for Apple's benefit, and were enforced through the threat of discipline. The Court also observed that Apple could tailor its bag-search policy as narrowly or broadly as it wished and could minimize search time by hiring sufficient security personnel or employing adequate security technology, but that it had to compensate employees to whom the policy applied for the time spent waiting for and undergoing the searches.

citations.quote: In sum, we reaffirm our holding in Morillion that “[t]he level of the employer’s control over its employees, rather than the mere fact that the employer requires the employees’ activity, is determinative” concerning whether an activity is compensable under the “hours worked” control clause.

We conclude that courts may and should consider additional relevant factors — including, but not limited to, the location of the activity, the degree of the employer’s control, whether the activity primarily benefits the employee or employer, and whether the activity is enforced through disciplinary measures

Apple’s exit searches are required as a practical matter, occur at the workplace, involve a significant degree of control, are imposed primarily for Apple’s benefit, and are enforced through threat of discipline.

We reiterate that Apple may tailor its bag-search policy as narrowly or broadly as it desires and may minimize the time required for exit searches by hiring sufficient security personnel or employing adequate security technology.

expectedJSON.gap: The factors quotation is cut off after the words "disciplinary measures" because the remainder of the Court's sentence ("when evaluating such employer-controlled conduct") is broken across a line in the slip-opinion text with a hyphenation artifact ("employer- controlled") that cannot be reproduced verbatim; the omitted words are paraphrased in the body. Frlekin's factor list is expressly non-exhaustive ("including, but not limited to"), and the Court framed it as applying to onsite employer-controlled activities; whether and how these factors apply to offsite activities was not decided.

expectedJSON.body: Apple asked the Court to apply its holding prospectively only, arguing that it had reasonably relied on Morillion as establishing that purely voluntary activities are not employer control. The Court rejected that argument, explaining that Morillion addressed compulsory employer-provided transportation and did not hold that an employer-controlled activity must be unavoidably required in order to count as "hours worked," so Apple could not claim reasonable reliance on settled law. The Court saw no reason to depart from the general rule that judicial decisions apply retroactively. Separately, because the Court found the search time compensable under the control clause, it expressed no view on the employees' alternative argument that the same time was compensable under the "suffered or permitted to work" clause.

citations.quote: Morillion addressed compulsory employer-provided transportation to and from work. (Morillion, supra, 22 Cal.4th at p. 578.) It did not, as Apple contends, hold that any employer-controlled activity must be unavoidably required in order to be compensable as “hours worked.”
Accordingly, we see no reason to depart from the general rule that judicial decisions apply retroactively.

Because we have concluded that plaintiffs are entitled to compensation under the control clause, we express no view concerning plaintiffs’ alternative argument that the searches are compensable under the “suffered or permitted to work” clause.

expectedJSON.gap: The retroactivity ruling means Frlekin's holding governs conduct that predates the February 13, 2020 decision, subject to any applicable limitations periods, which this document does not address. The Court's statement that it expressed no view on the "suffered or permitted to work" clause is a limitation on the reach of Frlekin's reasoning, not a holding that exit-search time is or is not compensable under that clause.

expectedJSON.body: In Huerta v. CSI Electrical Contractors, decided in 2024, the California Supreme Court applied the control clause to a construction worksite with a single security gate. Workers drove their personal vehicles to the gate, where guards scanned badges and sometimes looked inside vehicles and truck beds; at the end of the day workers again lined up at the gate for an exit procedure that could take a minute or more per vehicle and caused delays of five to over 30 minutes. The Court held that an employee's time spent on an employer's premises awaiting and undergoing an employer-mandated exit procedure that includes the employer's visual inspection of the employee's personal vehicle is compensable as "hours worked" within the meaning of Wage Order No. 16, section 2(J).

citations.cite: Cal. Supreme Court No. S275431 (Cal. Mar. 25, 2024)
citations.quote: The exit procedure could take up to a minute or more per vehicle and caused delays of five to over 30 minutes.

citations.cite: Cal. Supreme Court No. S275431 (Cal. Mar. 25, 2024)
citations.quote: First, an employee’s time spent on an employer’s premises awaiting and undergoing an employer-mandated exit procedure that includes the employer’s visual inspection of the employee’s personal vehicle is compensable as “hours worked” within the meaning of Wage Order No. 16, section 2(J).

expectedJSON.gap: Huerta answered questions certified by the Ninth Circuit under Wage Order No. 16 (on-site occupations in construction, drilling, logging, and mining); the "hours worked" definition it applied is the same two-clause definition found in the other wage orders. This clause cites the opinion by California Supreme Court docket number and decision date because the CourtListener record fetched for this document did not carry an official reporter citation, and no reporter citation was independently verified. The description of the gate procedure is taken from the Court's recitation of the facts as certified by the Ninth Circuit.

expectedJSON.body: Huerta also addressed the time employees spent driving their personal vehicles between the security gate and the employee parking lots while subject to site rules such as a 20-mile-per-hour speed limit and a prohibition on playing music that could be heard outside the vehicle. The Court gave two distinct answers. First, that travel is not compensable as "hours worked" under the control clause, because an employer's imposition of ordinary workplace rules on employees during their drive to the worksite in a personal vehicle does not create the requisite level of employer control. Second, the same travel may nonetheless be compensable under a separate provision found in Wage Order No. 16, section 5(A), which requires payment for all employer-mandated travel that occurs after the first location where the employee's presence is required by the employer. The Court held that the drive between the security gate and the parking lots is compensable as employer-mandated travel under section 5(A) if the security gate was the first location where the employee's presence was required for an employment-related reason other than the practical necessity of accessing the worksite.

citations.cite: Cal. Supreme Court No. S275431 (Cal. Mar. 25, 2024)
citations.quote: Separately, this travel time is not compensable as “hours worked” because an employer’s imposition of ordinary workplace rules on employees during their drive to the worksite in a personal vehicle does not create the requisite level of employer control.

citations.cite: Cal. Supreme Court No. S275431 (Cal. Mar. 25, 2024)
citations.quote: Second, the time that an employee spends traveling between the Security Gate and the employee parking lots is compensable as “employer-mandated travel” under Wage Order No. 16, section 5(A)

expectedJSON.gap: The section 5(A) employer-mandated-travel provision discussed in Huerta is specific to Wage Order No. 16; the Court's second answer therefore does not translate directly to employees governed by other wage orders that lack an equivalent provision. The section 5(A) holding is quoted from the opinion's introductory answer only through the words "section 5(A)" because the remainder of that sentence contains a slip-opinion line-break hyphenation artifact ("employment- related") that cannot be reproduced verbatim; the condition the Court attached (first location required for an employment-related reason other than the practical necessity of accessing the worksite) is paraphrased in the body. The characterization of the specific rules in effect during the drive (the speed limit and music restriction) is drawn from the opinion's statement of facts and is summarized rather than quoted.

expectedJSON.body: The third question in Huerta concerned employees covered by a collective bargaining agreement that satisfied Labor Code section 512, subdivision (e), and Wage Order No. 16, section 10(E), and that provided for an unpaid meal period, where the employer prohibited employees from leaving the premises during that period. The Court held that such time is nonetheless compensable under the wage order as "hours worked" if the employer prohibits the employee from leaving the employer's premises or a designated area during the meal period and if this prohibition prevents the employee from engaging in otherwise feasible personal activities. The Court added that an employee may bring an action under Labor Code section 1194 to enforce the wage order and recover unpaid wages for that time.

citations.cite: Cal. Supreme Court No. S275431 (Cal. Mar. 25, 2024)
citations.quote: that time is nonetheless compensable under the wage order as “hours worked” if the employer prohibits the employee from leaving the employer’s premises or a designated area during the meal period and if this prohibition prevents the employee from engaging in otherwise feasible personal activities. An employee may bring an action under Labor Code section 1194 to enforce the wage order and recover unpaid wages for that time.

expectedJSON.gap: This holding is framed around the collective-bargaining exemption in Labor Code section 512(e) and Wage Order 16 section 10(E); the Court's point was that a qualifying agreement's designation of a meal period as unpaid does not override the wage order's requirement to pay for time during which the employee remains under the employer's control. The general rules for meal periods outside that setting, including the premium pay for missed meal periods, are covered by the corpus's separate meal and rest break documents and are not restated here.

expectedJSON.body: Federal courts applying the Fair Labor Standards Act have sometimes excused payment for small amounts of otherwise compensable time under a "de minimis" doctrine, on a showing that the bits of time are administratively difficult to record. In Troester v. Starbucks Corp., the California Supreme Court answered a certified question about whether that federal doctrine applies to claims for unpaid wages under California Labor Code sections 510, 1194, and 1197. The facts involved a shift supervisor whom the employer's software required to clock out before running the store-closing procedure, activating the alarm, locking the door, and walking coworkers to their cars, amounting to several minutes of unpaid work per closing shift. The Court held that the relevant California statutes and wage order have not incorporated the FLSA de minimis doctrine, and that although California has a de minimis rule as a background principle of state law, that rule did not apply on these facts. The Court stated that the relevant statutes and wage order do not allow employers to require employees to routinely work for minutes off the clock without compensation, and observed that a few extra minutes of work each day can add up.

citations.quote: Federal courts have applied the doctrine in some circumstances to excuse the payment of wages for small amounts of otherwise compensable time upon a showing that the bits of time are administratively difficult to record.

We hold that the relevant California statutes and wage order have not incorporated the de minimis doctrine found in the FLSA. We further conclude that although California has a de minimis rule that is a background principle of state law, the rule is not applicable to the regularly reoccurring activities that are principally at issue here.
As the facts here demonstrate, a few extra minutes of work each day can add up.

expectedJSON.gap: The Court's concluding sentence about routine off-the-clock minutes is not quoted verbatim because the slip-opinion text breaks the word "off-the-clock" across a line ("off-the- clock"); it is paraphrased in the body. Troester's holding is limited to regularly occurring off-the-clock work of the kind before the Court; the next clause states what the Court expressly left open regarding irregular or very brief activities.

expectedJSON.body: Troester expressly left open whether there are wage claims involving employee activities that are so irregular or brief in duration that it would not be reasonable to require employers to compensate employees for the time spent on them. In declining to adopt the federal doctrine for regularly occurring work, the Court pointed to alternatives to leaving the time unpaid: restructuring the work so that employees do not have to work before or after clocking out; using technological advances that may help with tracking small amounts of time, including customizing available time-tracking tools or developing new ones; and, where neither restructuring nor a technological fix is practical, reasonably estimating work time — for example, through surveys, time studies, or a fair rounding policy — and compensating employees for that time. The Court declined to adopt a rule that would require the employee to bear the entire burden of any difficulty in recording regularly occurring work time.

citations.quote: We leave open whether there are wage claims involving employee activities that are so irregular or brief in duration that employers may not be reasonably required to compensate employees for the time spent on them.

technological advances may help with tracking small amounts of time. An employer may be able to customize and adapt available time tracking tools or develop new ones when no off-the-shelf product meets its needs. And even when neither a restructuring of work nor a technological fix is practical, it may be possible to reasonably estimate work time — for example, through surveys, time studies, or, as See’s Candy suggested, a fair rounding policy — and to compensate employees for that time.

expectedJSON.gap: The alternatives described here are the Court's own observations about how the recording difficulty that motivated the federal doctrine can be addressed; they are not a list of legal requirements, and the Court did not hold that any particular method must be used. The reference to a "fair rounding policy" points to See's Candy Shops, Inc. v. Superior Court, whose rounding standard — and the later limits placed on it — are described in the separate Time Clock Rounding Practices information sheet.

expectedJSON.body: Time that qualifies as "hours worked" under the control clause must be paid at no less than the applicable minimum wage and, where it pushes the employee past the daily or weekly overtime thresholds, at the applicable overtime rate. Labor Code section 1194, subdivision (a), provides that, notwithstanding any agreement to work for a lesser wage, any employee receiving less than the legal minimum wage or the legal overtime compensation applicable to the employee is entitled to recover in a civil action the unpaid balance of the full amount of that minimum wage or overtime compensation, including interest, reasonable attorney's fees, and costs of suit. The California Supreme Court in Huerta identified section 1194 as the vehicle by which an employee may enforce the wage order and recover unpaid wages for time spent under the employer's control, and Troester was itself framed as a question about claims under sections 510, 1194, and 1197.

citations.quote: Notwithstanding any agreement to work for a lesser wage, any employee receiving less than the legal minimum wage or the legal overtime compensation applicable to the employee is entitled to recover in a civil action the unpaid balance of the full amount of this minimum wage or overtime compensation, including interest thereon, reasonable attorney’s fees, and costs of suit.

citations.cite: Cal. Supreme Court No. S275431 (Cal. Mar. 25, 2024)
citations.quote: An employee may bring an action under Labor Code section 1194 to enforce the wage order and recover unpaid wages for that time.

expectedJSON.gap: Section 1194 is the civil-action remedy; wage claims may also be pursued administratively before the Labor Commissioner, and other Labor Code provisions (for example, liquidated damages under section 1194.2 and civil penalties under the Private Attorneys General Act) may be implicated but are not covered here. The overtime calculation rules themselves are described in the separate California Overtime Pay Calculation information sheet.
